title: Stock control
summary: Regular inventories give you the cost of what was consumed and reveal shortages that would otherwise go unnoticed.

sections.heading: What inventories are for
items: Working out the cost of goods consumed.
Seeing what needs restocking and planning purchases.

sections.heading: The cost of what was consumed
paragraphs: Opening inventory + purchases in the period − closing inventory = cost of goods consumed. Both inventories are counted and valued with the same method.
A spreadsheet or accounting system gives you that figure, which then feeds the income statement and the pricing coefficient.

sections.heading: Spotting shortages
paragraphs: If you write down what was recorded in orders or invoices next to the consumption according to inventory, you can compare both. A difference means unrecorded shortages, stock leaks or billing errors.
Sometimes procedures need to change and sometimes action must be taken with staff or outsiders. Without stock control, you never find out what's going on.

sections.heading: Raw material yield
paragraphs: Choosing the right size of what you buy (a plant, a bird, a cut) is also cost control: the same product can yield perfectly for one dish or cause heavy losses if the size isn't right.
